title: The Smile of Marrow Creek
premise: Coral Hartwell arrives in Marrow Creek to appraise the Aldergate house for a probate sale, but the property's measurements refuse to stay consistent, and the house seems to appraise its visitors in return. When Coral's sleep-recording app captures a second voice answering questions Coral never asked aloud, they realize the house has been counting its residents for a hundred years — and the last surviving Aldergate heir, Wren, is due to sign the sale papers that will seal the final resident inside. Falling for Wren against every professional instinct, Coral must falsify their own survey, break the count, and get Wren out of the county before the signing — ending with the house left standing, empty and patient, and Coral's recordings of the second voice deliberately preserved as the only memorial it will ever get.
about_author: Isandro Thackeray is the pen name of a former county land assessor who spent eleven years walking the property lines of dying mill towns before turning to fiction. They live near a reservoir that submerged three villages, and they still keep field notebooks.

chapters.title: Chain of Title
chapters.summary: Coral Hartwell, POV. Coral arrives in Marrow Creek to appraise the Aldergate house for probate, documenting every room with methodical care. The emotional beat is quiet unease: the deed history shows the house has been sold, inherited, and re-sold eleven times, yet every transfer lists the same notary. Coral's documentation-as-prayer ritual is established.

chapters.title: The Measurements Drift
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral's laser measurements of the parlor disagree with themselves by inches, then feet, depending on which direction they shoot. A neighbor, Odile, warns them to finish the survey in daylight only. The beat is professional pride curdling into denial as Coral re-measures and blames their equipment.

chapters.title: Wren Aldergate
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral meets Wren, the last heir, who has returned reluctantly to sign the sale papers. Wren is brittle, sarcastic, and clearly terrified of the house in a way they won't explain. The beat is reluctant attraction — two strangers both pretending this is just a transaction.

chapters.title: Eleven Residents
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. In the county archive, Coral finds census records: the house has always held exactly eleven residents, across every decade, no matter how many people actually lived there. The beat is dread arriving through paperwork — Coral's own language of documentation turning against them.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Reviewing their sleep-recording app out of boredom, Coral hears a second voice answering questions Coral never asked — calm, patient, asking Coral to 'state your condition for the record.' The beat is violation and fascination; Coral plays the file eleven times.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. The neighbor reveals her family kept a ledger of the count for four generations: every resident the house 'appraised' — measured, valued, and kept. Her grandmother was the twelfth, removed by force, and never slept a whole night again. The beat is inherited guilt and a warning Coral doesn't fully heed.

chapters.title: Appraised Back
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. The house begins responding to Coral's survey: rooms Coral documents are clean and warm; rooms Coral skips decay overnight. Coral realizes the appraisal is mutual — the house is pricing them. The beat is the horror of being valued, and the first admission that this is not a job.

chapters.title: What Wren Signed
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren's chapter reveals their childhood: the house counted them from birth, and their mother stayed 'voluntarily' until the count was complete. Wren fled at seventeen and has been running from the signing ever since. The beat is shame and the fear that belonging here is the only belonging they've ever had.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Has a Name
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Cross-referencing the sleep recordings with the ledger, Coral identifies the voice: Hesper Aldergate, appraised in 1923, the count's keeper. Hesper begins addressing Coral directly in the recordings — politely, terribly — asking Coral to 'confirm the total.' The beat is intimacy with something inhuman.

chapters.title: Duty of Disclosure
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral's firm calls: the sale closes in nine days, and any irregularity in the survey voids their license. Coral faces the choice — report the anomalies and trigger an investigation that traps Wren in the county, or falsify the appraisal. The beat is duty versus conscience, the theme of love against duty made concrete.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Coral and Wren, alternating POV. They plan the falsified survey together, and the collaboration becomes courtship — measuring rooms at dawn, lying to lawyers, sharing the sleep recordings like love letters. The beat is warmth inside dread; the house, notably, stops decaying the rooms they share.

chapters.title: Hesper's Offer
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. In the deepest recording yet, Hesper makes her case: the house keeps its residents from being forgotten. She offers Coral a place in the count — valued, permanent, remembered forever. The beat is temptation; Coral, who documents everything because they fear being unrecorded, nearly says yes.

chapters.title: The Twelfth Room
chapters.summary: Coral and Wren, POV shared. Following Hesper's measurements, they find a room that appears on no floor plan — the room where the counted wait. Inside: eleven chairs, one occupied by something that has been patient for a century. The beat is awe and horror fused; Wren recognizes their mother's coat on the chair.

chapters.title: Wren's Mother
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. The occupant is not quite their mother — a memory of her, maintained by the house, who begs Wren to stay and complete the count so she can rest. The beat is grief weaponized into a trap; Wren must refuse the one voice they've missed most.

chapters.title: Falsifying the Prayer
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral submits the falsified appraisal — declaring the house structurally worthless, unmarketable, condemned by subsidence. The beat is self-betrayal as sacrifice: Coral burns their professional credibility, the thing that made them feel real, to buy Wren time.

chapters.title: The Firm Objects
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral's firm sends a senior surveyor to re-inspect, and the house performs for him — measurements true, rooms immaculate. The senior surveyor declares Coral incompetent and schedules a new appraisal on the original closing date. The beat is gaslighting at institutional scale; Coral's documentation, their prayer, is dismissed as error.

chapters.title: Odile's Debt
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile reveals the ledger's final page: the count can be broken only if a resident is appraised and refused — valued fully, then rejected by the house itself. Her grandmother failed because the house never refused anyone. The beat is desperate hope with a hidden cost neither of them sees yet.

chapters.title: State Your Condition
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral answers Hesper's questions on the recording, deliberately — offering themselves for appraisal in Wren's place. Hesper measures Coral across three nights of dreams: every fear, every loneliness, every reason they document the world. The beat is terrible intimacy; Coral lets themselves be fully known by something that keeps what it values.

chapters.title: The Count of Eleven
chapters.summary: Climax, Coral and Wren, alternating POV. On the closing date, the house completes Coral's appraisal — and refuses them, because Coral's value lies in leaving, in carrying the record out. Enraged, the count turns to Wren, the last resident, as the papers arrive for signature. Wren stands in the twelfth room with the pen; Coral, locked in the hall, screams the truth Hesper cannot record: Wren was never appraised at all — the house never counted what it loved.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren tears up the papers and walks out through every room, naming each one aloud — refusing the house room by room, an appraisal in reverse. The count breaks at ten; the twelfth room empties; the mother-memory dissolves with something like gratitude. The beat is cathartic grief and the first free breath Wren has taken since childhood.

chapters.title: Closing Costs
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. The house stands empty, unsold, off every ledger Coral's firm can find. Coral has lost their license, their career, their certainties. But the sleep recordings still hold Hesper's voice — and Coral chooses not to delete them, preserving the count's memory the only way it can now exist. The beat is mourning and quiet resolve.

chapters.title: The New Ledger
chapters.summary: Coral and Wren, shared POV, epilogue. Months later, Coral and Wren live in Marrow Creek — in Odile's house, two doors down, never the Aldergate house. Coral keeps field notebooks again, and Wren has started writing the true history of the eleven. The last line: some nights, the recorder catches a third voice, faint and content, saying only 'noted.' The beat is belonging chosen, not counted.
